projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Yes. My wife and children are here with me. As regards my eyes I have had seven attacks of irido-ciclitis, a consequence of malarial fever which I got in Rome after a drenching on the Pincio. It comes on suddenly and incapacitates me for work for five or four weeks. Lately I seem better but it comes without warning. Yes, I need work and want it if I can get it. I mean here in Switzerland . My work is teaching. I have two degrees: Dublin & Padua . I hope to get something here or in Lausanne or Geneva when the scholastic year begins. I am (or was) till it closed teacher in the Higher School of Commerce in Trieste and have also that certificate. Journalism is not my line. I sent the facts of the case as you wished. If that fund sends me any subvention I can assure you it will be much appreciated. I cannot find any work here. The situation would be indeed bad if I had not hopes that your intervention and Yeats’s will do me some good. As a matter of fact we have not sufficient clothes. The summer here is quite cold in comparison with Trieste. I did not send these details to Mr Pinker because I know him so slightly and because, if my case became known, I am at a disadvantage with publishers. I send him tonight the first act of Exiles
and ask him to let you have the MS to read. I certainly owe you this at least, and shall value your opinion highly. I hope and believe that you will do what you can to enable me to live on here in Switzerland till these bad times are over and till I begin to receive something for my writing.

div.note: Iridocyclitis is an inflammation of the iris (the colored part of the eye behind the cornea) and of the muscles and tissue that control the focusing of the eye. After returning to Trieste from a seven-month stay in Rome in 1906-1907, where he worked in a bank, JJ came down with rheumatic fever, which he suspected may have resulted from “his carefree nights in Roman and Triestine gutters” (Ellmann, JJ 262).

The Pincian Hill, or Pincio, is a hill in the historical center of Rome. JJ described it early on in his Roman sojourn as “a fine garden overlooking one gate of the city” (LII 145). It was also, less idyllically, the scene of a nocturnal drinking bout with two mailmen with whom JJ went carousing (Ellmann, JJ 241-42). JJ had a long history of eye ailments and acutely painful attacks. His first operation, an iridectomy, was performed in Zurich in 1917.
JJ was not interested in an offer Ford Madox Hueffer had made to get him a job in the War Office working in the censorship department (see JJ to Pound, 14 July 1915, notes.

JJ received his Bachelor of Arts degree from University College Dublin (UCD) in 1902, where he had studied modern languages and other subjects. Desiring to teach in an Italian public school, he took a series of examinations offered by the Italian government at the University of Padua in April 1912. He passed easily, but the validity of his exam results was annulled when Italian officials refused to recognize reciprocity with UCD (Louis Berrone, “Two James Joyce Essays Unveiled: ‘The Centenary of Charles Dickens’ and ‘L’influenza letteraria universale del rinascimento,’” Journal of Modern Literature, vol. 5, no. 1 [1976]: 3-18).
JJ taught English in Trieste, first at a Berlitz School and later, beginning in 1913, at the Scuola Superiore di Commercio Revoltella, a commercial high school, as well as in private lessons.

In an effort to obtain a subsistence grant for JJ from the Royal Literary Fund, Pound had asked him for the facts of his current situation in a letter of circa 10 July 1915 (Pound/Joyce 36). JJ replied on 14 July 1915. For details of the Fund and the £75 grant that JJ received, see JJ to Pound, 14 July 1915, notes.
W.B. Yeats was one of several influential persons who helped JJ receive a grant from the Royal Literary Fund (see JJ to Pound, 14 July 1915, notes).

JJ wrote his London literary agent J.B. Pinker on 17 July 1915 with an update about efforts to secure a grant from the Royal Literary Fund, and other matters (LII 353). Pound wrote Yeats circa 22 July 1915 that JJ did not want his straitened circumstances widely known, as this “would place him at a disadvantage with publishers,” adding, “As I dare say it would, the lice!” (LII 354).

JJ was arranging to have his play Exiles typed and sent to Pinker in installments (see JJ to Pound, 14 July 1915, notes). Pound read Exiles and wrote JJ a long letter circa 7 September 1915 to say that the play was “interesting” and “exciting” but that no audience “could follow it or take it in,” and no manager “would stage it in our chaste and castrated english speaking world.” Pound felt that the play “works up quite a whirl of emotion, and it has, undoubtedly, form,” but he did not think it “nearly as intense as ‘The Portrait.’” With remarkable prescience, he added, “When you are a recognized classic people will read it because you wrote it and be duly interested and duly instructed” (LII 365-66). Pound pursued these insights further in “Mr. James Joyce and the Modern Stage,” Drama, vol. 6, no. 2 (February 1916): 122-32, where he observed that Exiles “has inner form [and] the acts and speeches of one person work into the acts and speeches of another and make the play into an indivisible, integral whole.” Yet he thought it “unstageable, precisely because the closeness and cogency of the [intellectual-emotional] process is, as I think, too great for an audience to be able to follow … under present conditions.
